meta.title: Your Interactive Voter Guide
meta.disclaimer: This is an independent, non-partisan guide. Candidate and measure summaries are synthesized from a mix of non-partisan sources (Ballotpedia, CalMatters, LAist, the official Voter Information Guide, Wikipedia), left-leaning outlets, and right-leaning outlets, and are written to inform rather than to endorse. Where independent coverage is limited (many minor candidates and judicial races), only ballot-listed facts are shown. Always confirm against your official ballot and lavote.gov.

contests.office: Mayor — City of Los Angeles
contests.note: Nonpartisan office. Top two advance to the November runoff unless someone wins a majority.

candidates.name: Spencer Pratt
candidates.blurb: Reality-TV personality ('The Hills') turned political newcomer who built a large social-media following after the January 2025 Palisades Fire. Running as a conservative outsider, he campaigns on public safety and mental health. Polled at 22% in the final pre-election Berkeley IGS/LA Times survey.

candidates.name: Adam Miller
candidates.blurb: Tech entrepreneur who self-funded his campaign with $4 million. He advocates for increasing the LAPD to over 10,000 officers and focuses on fiscal management and accountability.

candidates.name: Juanita Lopez
candidates.blurb: Political scientist who was the first to qualify for the ballot. She campaigns as a 'common-sense' alternative, focusing on law and order (enforcing no-littering laws), lowering the city sales tax to 8%, and quarterly budget transparency.

candidates.name: John Logsdon
candidates.blurb: Neighborhood Council member and producer/director. He focuses on expanding the LAPD, improving 911 response times, and criticized the city's response to the 2025 Palisades fire.

candidates.name: Nithya Raman
candidates.blurb: City Councilmember and urban planner who entered the race late, arguing the city is at a 'breaking point.' She advocates for 60-day zoning approvals and tenant protections. Polled at 25% in the final pre-election Berkeley IGS/LA Times survey.

candidates.name: Tish Hyman
candidates.blurb: Grammy-nominated songwriter and musician running as an outsider. Her platform focuses on women's safety in public spaces, mental health rehabilitation, and auditing homelessness funds.

candidates.name: Rae Chen Huang
candidates.blurb: Community organizer and pastor who has polled competitively at ~9%. She focuses on homelessness and affordability, advocating for community-led solutions.

candidates.name: Karen Ruth Bass
candidates.blurb: Incumbent mayor seeking a second term, highlighting her 'Inside Safe' program. She led the final pre-election Berkeley IGS/LA Times survey with 26%, placing her in a statistical tie with her top challengers.

candidates.name: Nelson Cheng
candidates.blurb: Roblox YouTuber and behavioral interventionist representing youth and education. He proposes converting warehouses into shelters and making Metro buses free during peak commute hours.

candidates.name: Andrej A. Selivra
candidates.blurb: Systems engineer and UCLA graduate who experienced teenage homelessness. He proposes 'Dormitory Style' public housing in underused commercial buildings and a 'MetroX' sprinter van shuttle service.

candidates.name: Asaad Alnajjar
candidates.ballotOccupation: Engineering Manager, City of Los Angeles
candidates.blurb: City engineering manager and neighborhood councilor running as an experienced public servant.

candidates.name: Bryant Acosta
candidates.blurb: Nightlife promoter and event producer from the queer community. He proposes the 'LA NOW' app for real-time transparency, vacancy taxes on empty units, and city-run food markets.

candidates.name: Suzy Kim
candidates.blurb: Mental health professional working with LAPD's SMART teams. She focuses on mental health crisis response and integrating social services with public safety.

candidates.name: Andrew K. Kim
candidates.blurb: Civil rights attorney running on an 'Anti-Woke' platform. He supports strict enforcement of anti-camping laws and a 'recovery first' policy for mental health and addiction.

candidates.name: Write-In Candidate
candidates.blurb: You may write in any qualified write-in candidate. Qualified write-ins are posted by the elections office shortly before the election.

contests.office: City Attorney — City of Los Angeles
contests.note: Nonpartisan office.

candidates.name: John McKinney
candidates.blurb: Veteran Deputy District Attorney with nearly 30 years of experience. He campaigns on a 'law and order' platform with 'compassionate accountability' for homelessness, focusing on public safety and prosecuting repeat offenders. Endorsed by the LAPPL and DA Nathan Hochman.

candidates.name: Marissa Roy
candidates.blurb: Deputy State Attorney General and former Deputy City Attorney running as a progressive challenger. She promises to transform the office into a public-interest law firm, focusing on tenant protections, wage theft, and suing tech companies. Endorsed by Bernie Sanders and the LA County Democrats.

candidates.name: Hydee Feldstein Soto
candidates.blurb: Incumbent City Attorney seeking re-election on her record of restructuring the office and enforcing rules of law. She highlights her efforts in the Figueroa corridor and upholding anti-camping laws, while facing criticism over eviction protection services and use of outside counsel.

candidates.name: Aida Ashouri
candidates.blurb: Human rights and legal aid attorney. She campaigns on a 'people over profits' platform, promising to reopen code enforcement and environmental units to prosecute 'slumlords' and polluters, and emphasizing police accountability.

candidates.name: Write-In Candidate
candidates.blurb: You may write in any qualified write-in candidate.

contests.office: Controller — City of Los Angeles
contests.note: Nonpartisan office. The Controller is the city's independent financial watchdog and auditor.

candidates.name: Kenneth Mejia
candidates.blurb: Incumbent Controller and CPA running on 'radical transparency.' He highlights his use of public dashboards for tracking city spending and auditing the LAPD, while facing criticism over workplace culture and his use of office branding.

candidates.name: Zach Sokoloff
candidates.blurb: Finance executive and 'common-sense' challenger who argues for 'results over reports.' He focuses on 2028 Olympics oversight, homelessness service coordination, and has received significant financial backing from independent expenditure committees. Endorsed by former Controller Laura Chick.

candidates.name: Write-In Candidate

candidates.blurb: Incumbent Councilmember and chair of the Budget and Finance Committee. She highlights a reduction in street homelessness in her district, advocates for more interim housing, and supports phasing out residential oil drilling. She recently survived a recall attempt over a homeless housing project.

candidates.name: Morgan Oyler

contests.title: Measure CB
contests.subtitle: LA City — cannabis business taxes on unlicensed businesses
contests.summary: Applies the City of Los Angeles's existing cannabis business taxes (10% on cannabis sales, 5% on medical cannabis, 2% on manufacturing/cultivation, 1% on transportation/testing/research) to unlicensed cannabis businesses. The City estimates roughly $30–35 million per year for general city services. Proponents argue it provides an enforcement tool to pressure illegal shops, while critics worry it legitimizes unlicensed operators.

options.label: YES on Measure CB
options.blurb: Supporters, including legal business owners, argue it levels the playing field and provides an 'Al Capone' style enforcement tool—taxing illegal shops that the city has struggled to shut down through licensing alone.

options.label: NO on Measure CB
options.blurb: Opponents, including Social Equity LA, argue this 'normalizes' illegal shops and signals they are permanent. Critics also call the strategy 'incoherent,' questioning the city's attempt to collect taxes from businesses it aims to close.

contests.title: Measure TC
contests.subtitle: LA City — transient occupancy (hotel) tax on online travel companies
contests.summary: Updates the City's Transient Occupancy Tax so online travel companies (Expedia, Booking.com, Airbnb) must collect and remit the hotel tax on the full service charges and fees they add when booking a room—closing a collection loophole. Estimated to generate about $5 million per year. Works together with Measure TT.

options.label: YES on Measure TC
options.blurb: Supporters, including a unanimous City Council, say it modernizes the tax code to ensure guests are taxed on the actual price paid, regardless of whether they book directly or through a third-party platform.

options.label: NO on Measure TC
options.blurb: No formal opposition argument was submitted for the official ballot. A 'No' vote leaves the current collection rules unchanged, allowing booking sites to continue paying tax only on wholesale rates.

contests.title: Measure TT
contests.subtitle: LA City — hotel tax change to fund city services
contests.summary: Raises the City's hotel tax by 2% (to 16%) through Dec 31, 2028, to fund services ahead of the 2028 Olympics, then sets it at 15% permanently starting Jan 1, 2029. The City estimates about $44 million per year through 2028 and about $22 million per year afterward. Works together with Measure TC.

options.label: YES on Measure TT
options.blurb: Supporters argue the increase is 'jet fuel' for 2028 Olympics preparation, funding essential city services like fire protection, parks, and street repair using revenue from visitors rather than residents.

options.label: NO on Measure TT
options.blurb: Opponents, including the Central City Association, worry a higher tax makes LA less competitive, driving tourists to nearby cities like Burbank or Culver City and potentially threatening local tourism jobs.

Endorsed by the LA County Democrats and Planned Parenthood.

candidates.blurb: Software engineer and startup founder running as a data-driven outsider. He proposes a 'unified command' for emergency shelters and advocates for restoring consequences for crime while reducing reliance on non-profit contractors.

candidates.name: Tonia Arey
candidates.blurb: Real estate agent and community activist focusing on public safety and fire recovery. She advocates for fully funding the Sheriff's department, fast-tracking permits for fire rebuilding, and opposes the 'Housing First' model. Endorsed by the LAGOP and Alex Villanueva.

contests.title: County Measure ER
contests.subtitle: Essential Services Restoration Act — LA County general sales tax
contests.summary: A temporary one-half-cent (0.5%) increase to the Los Angeles County sales tax for five years (expiring Oct 2031), estimated to raise $1 billion per year to backfill federal Medi-Cal cuts and protect public hospitals and health-care programs. Groceries and prescriptions are exempt.

options.label: YES on Measure ER
options.blurb: Supporters, including public hospitals and unions, argue the tax is crucial to protect the healthcare safety net from federal funding cuts, preventing hospital closures and ensuring access for 700,000 residents.

options.label: NO on Measure ER
options.blurb: Opponents, including taxpayer groups and a coalition of 18 cities, argue sales taxes are regressive and that LA's tax is already too high. Critics also note it's a 'general tax' with no guarantee of where the money is spent.
